utterances.text: Do you remember the locations?

utterances.speaker: AJMAN AWAD [Resumed]
utterances.text: As far as I know, in the area of Tesanj, Zesjelno Polje [phoen], even at a later stage at Gluha Bukovica. Yes, Gluha Bukovica. I even think in Kalesija, in Tuzla, he had a group. That's the ones I can recall.

utterances.speaker: MS. VIDOVIC
utterances.text: Could you please describe the physical appearance of that person if you know him?

utterances.speaker: AJMAN AWAD [Resumed]
utterances.text: He's heavily built and a large man, a big man, a tall man. I am not familiar with the details. I did see him, but I didn't have any contact with him, so I don't know any more details about it.

utterances.speaker: MS. VIDOVIC
utterances.text: Would you agree that he was above average -- of above-average build and weight?

utterances.speaker: AJMAN AWAD [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. He was really a heavy man.

utterances.speaker: MS. VIDOVIC
utterances.text: These groups of Abu Zubeir's, they had nothing to do with the El Mujahedin Detachment, did they?

utterances.speaker: AJMAN AWAD [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, they didn't.

utterances.speaker: MS. VIDOVIC
utterances.text: They did not accept the El Mujahedin Detachment?

utterances.speaker: AJMAN AWAD [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, that's right.

utterances.speaker: MS. VIDOVIC
utterances.text: They never became a part of the army, to the best of your knowledge?

utterances.speaker: AJMAN AWAD [Resumed]
utterances.text: To the best of my knowledge they didn't form separate units and became a part of the army. That's as much as I don't know -- as I know. I don't know whether they belonged to some unit or not.

utterances.speaker: MS. VIDOVIC
utterances.text: Very well. Why did Abu Zubeir not accept the El Mujahedin?

utterances.speaker: AJMAN AWAD [Resumed]
utterances.text: Abu Zubeir was in Tesanj, and when the road was liberated, they were able to come to Zenica from Tesanj. I remember that Abu Mali offered him the possibility of the Mujahedins to join forces and for him to become a part of the detachment and for us to work together. We would be bigger, better, and so on. However, he insisted on having a role in the leadership, for him to be the leader in the detachment. However, the detachment commander would not accept -- accept that, so that nothing came of it and they broke up.

utterances.speaker: MS. VIDOVIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Answering questions from the Prosecution, you spoke of combat activities in Vozuca in September 1995. It's right, isn't it, that Abu Zubeir, with his groups, did take part in combat operations at Vozuca in 1995?

utterances.speaker: AJMAN AWAD [Resumed]
utterances.text: I heard that they were present at Vozuca. I personally didn't see them. I didn't have occasion to see them. I said I was at the forward command post, so I didn't have any -- many contacts on the ground.

utterances.speaker: MS. VIDOVIC
utterances.text: But you heard that they did take part in these combat activities in the area of Vozuca?

utterances.speaker: AJMAN AWAD [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. VIDOVIC
utterances.text: To the best of your knowledge did -- they did not participate together with the El Mujahedin Detachment?

utterances.speaker: AJMAN AWAD [Resumed]
utterances.text: If they had, I would have known. They certainly didn't participate with the El Mujahedin Detachment.

utterances.speaker: MS. VIDOVIC
utterances.text: Did you hear of a Mujahedin camp in the village of Borovnica?

utterances.speaker: AJMAN AWAD [Resumed]
utterances.text: The detachment didn't have a camp in Borovnica. The El Mujahedin Detachment did not have a camp in the village of Borovnica.

utterances.speaker: MS. VIDOVIC
utterances.text: Did you perhaps hear who did have a camp in the Borovnica village?

utterances.speaker: AJMAN AWAD [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't know exactly. I know there were some Mujahedin there. I think it was Abu Zubeir's group. I think so, but I can't say with certainty.

utterances.speaker: MS. VIDOVIC
utterances.text: Thank you. I would now like to ask you something else. You told us yesterday that after the events in Guca Gora that you were involved in that you had agreed to draft a proposal to the 3rd Corps of the BH army to join the army. In fact, you said that you yourself had written that document in which you described the composition of the detachment. Am I right?

utterances.speaker: AJMAN AWAD [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. I -- I translated that request into Bosnian, and I personally delivered it at the protocol of the 3rd Corps headquarters.

utterances.speaker: MS. VIDOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Could the witness now look at Exhibit 67, please. Could the witness look at the second page straight away, please, of the Bosnian version, and the English version, for us to gain time. For the record, that is document entitled "Overview of the El Mujahedin Detachment and a list of members of the unit."

utterances.speaker: MS. VIDOVIC
utterances.text: Witness, would you please have a look at the first page.

utterances.speaker: AJMAN AWAD [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. VIDOVIC
utterances.text: And I want to ask you the following: Is this the document that you testified about yesterday, that you had written it? That is the proposal.

utterances.speaker: AJMAN AWAD [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, that is not that document. The document was not typed. I wrote it in longhand. We didn't have a typewriter, so I wrote everything by hand. It was handwritten. On the right hand was the Arabic text, and on the left was the Bosnian text. And I handed in at the protocol.

utterances.speaker: MS. VIDOVIC
utterances.text: So that is not this document. So it would be wrong to believe that this is -- this document is the proposal filed by the El Mujahedin Detachment of the 3rd Corps; is that right?

utterances.speaker: AJMAN AWAD [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. VIDOVIC
utterances.text: Nevertheless, I wish to ask you something in connection with this document. Under number 11 your name is mentioned: "Abu Ajman, assistant commander for security." And you told us that that should be you. Isn't that right? "Abu Ajman."

utterances.speaker: AJMAN AWAD [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. VIDOVIC
utterances.text: But you told us yesterday that you never performed those duties; is that right?

utterances.speaker: AJMAN AWAD [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. VIDOVIC
utterances.text: Do you agree then that this document does not reflect the real state of affairs and relationships within the detachment on the basis of what was said about you?

utterances.speaker: AJMAN AWAD [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. I even see some names, some companies. That certainly wasn't like that.

utterances.speaker: MS. VIDOVIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Will you now look at the note written by hand. Will you please look at it. The --

utterances.speaker: MS. VIDOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Could the English version be scrolled down for Their Honours to be see -- able to see it on the screen.

utterances.speaker: MS. VIDOVIC
utterances.text: And, Witness, would you look at it. And one would say it says: "Request all data, including passport numbers and the country of issuance of the passport." Do you see that written there?

utterances.speaker: AJMAN AWAD [Resumed]
utterances.text: I can't read it, but that would be it more or less.

utterances.speaker: MS. VIDOVIC
utterances.text: Yes. That's better now. Can you read it now? Can you see it better now?

utterances.speaker: AJMAN AWAD [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. VIDOVIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Witness, I wish to refer to this handwritten note and to ask you would you agree that the command of the detachment never provided copies of passports and the other data regarding the countries of origin of the foreigners to the corps command?

utterances.speaker: AJMAN AWAD [Resumed]
utterances.text: As far as I know, no copies were ever provided, copies of passports or other documents, of foreign volunteers or Mujahedin. What was provided was the real names and data of those members who wished to have this provided, when the individual insisted on this. However, passport copies were never provided to the command of the 3rd Corps of the army of Bosnia and Herzegovina, never.

utterances.speaker: MS. VIDOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honour --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Can I -- you told us that the name Hamza means a messenger who was a martyr, is that it? What does the name Abu mean? I see on this, Exhibit 67, everybody there is called Abu, including yourself. What does Abu mean?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Let me explain. I said Hamza is a name of the uncle of the messenger who was killed in the second battle in the history of Islam, and -- and the prophet Muhammad said of him that he was the champion of the shaheeds, people who were killed fighting for Islam and who went to paradise. The word "Abu" means "father." "Abu Hamza" means "Hamza's father." Among us Arabs, it is customary to give people names on the basis of their sons or their fathers. For instance, I personally am Abu Abdul Rahman, because my late father's name was Abdul Rahman, and I was given the name on the basis of the name of my father. Or a person without such a nickname may be named after his first child. Very often Muslims wish to have the -- the -- to be honoured by being named after the first shaheed, or martyr, and that is why he's called Abu Hamza.

utterances.speaker: MS. VIDOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you. Your Honour, I hope I'll manage to show the witness one more document. Could the witness be shown D765.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HARHOFF
utterances.text: While we wait for this document to come on the screen, can I just confirm with you that the purpose of -- of this last document we saw was to show that the 3rd Corps was never given any information of the identity of any of the members of the END? Is that correct? Can you confirm this, Mr. Awad?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] When I said that we didn't provide copies of our passports as a copy of -- of a document was never provided, but if somebody wanted to have his real first and second name to be on the list, it would be put on the name [as interpreted]. You may have read here Abu Ajman, for instance, or Abu, just Abu. In 1995, for me to acquire citizenship, I had to have a document with my real name indicated. I had to provide my original data that corresponded to do passport, though I didn't provide the passport, to be able to realise any rights. So some individuals did provide their data. From the first day I said I was Ajman Awad. I never said I was -- I had any other names. But somebody ask why Abu. Everyone was Abu, so they called me Abu Ajman. They always called me Abu Ajman. So you see, what was provided to the corps were the names Abu, Abu, Abu, except for those who explicitly wanted their real names to be provided. They provided data without providing passport copies. So they were responsible for the data they provided. Have I made myself clear?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HARHOFF
utterances.text: Yes and no. If you look at the following pages of the document that we have just put back, there are a lot of names that appear to be the real names, so to say, of -- of the members. I don't see any Abu anywhere. Oh, yes, do, later on.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honour, Judge, you're right, but these are Bosniaks.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HARHOFF
utterances.text: Yes, I see. But does this then mean that as of person number 111, in fact all the way to almost 186, all those names were not revealing the true identity of the persons? Is that how we should understand this?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] These persons were identified as such. Each one of them had a nickname. For instance, I don't know the real names of members of the detachment. I knew a couple of people. If we go back to this list, I see Abu Hubada [phoen], Abu Abaz or something. The real name is not here, only the nickname that each of them had. This considered the nickname to be their real identity for some, but as I was called Abu Abdul Rahman, it is my identity, but my real name is Ajman Awad. But if you say Abdul Rahman Awad, then it is me that is implied. I am implied.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HARHOFF
utterances.text: Can the Court conclude that the names indicated here in the last part of the list were sufficient to identify these individuals by their nickname and by their date of birth so that there would be no uncertainty as to who they were? You see, the reason we're asking this question is, of course, that if the El Mujahedin Detachment became part of the ABiH, then the ABiH would have a natural interest in knowing precisely who was part of their army. So that's why I'm interested in knowing whether the information offered in this list would provide sufficient information about the identity of these people. That's one possibility. The other possibility is that it would not, because this would only be nicknames while the true identity of the persons were still concealed. So I'm testing you on -- on the quality of information provided on the list.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I will explain why this is so. There are certain objective considerations. People who came from abroad to assist and to join in the fighting here in Bosnia and Herzegovina, they feared that if they gave their real identity, because there were many intelligence services -- I've seen documents when talking to the Prosecutor how the intelligence listened in to our conversations. If the Bosnian intelligence service were listening -- tapping us, what were the foreign intelligences doing? So many feared that their -- if their names were to be heard in their own countries, then their parents would have problems on the part of our own authorities over there, and that is why they did not wish to reveal their real names. They wanted only to use their nicknames. Among members within the detachment it was safe. There were no problem. However, I can understand your question. The authorities wished to have the real identity, the name, the number of the passport and everything, but this could not be done because of these fears. Those who had no fears did provide their data. I personally have problems on this account. Until I received BH citizenship, I didn't have any problems in Syria. I came here as a student, and there are no proceedings against me in Syria. However, when it was heard that I had acquired citizenship because of my participation here, I had problems. And my father was called in for interviews on several occasions, and my brothers, too, were called in by the security services for interviews because I was in Bosnia-Herzegovina and because I was a member of the army of Bosnia and Herzegovina. I think -- I hope I have explained now why this is so.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HARHOFF
utterances.text: You have. Thank you very much.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LATTANZI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Could we know the date of this document, because I have a question here for the members who were Bosniaks. Here we have an indication of the date. I suppose the date when they joined the army, whereas for the foreign members there are no such indications. Therefore, could one establish the date of this document?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I really don't know.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LATTANZI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] In view of the fact that it is Madam Vidovic who asked for this document to be used, could she tell us the date, please?

utterances.speaker: MS. VIDOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honour, this is an exhibit which was tendered by the Prosecutor. It had number 67. There is no date except for number 3 that you can see on this page. You can look at page number 3. You can see 001/93. And on the basis of that and the date later, you can conclude that this is a document from 1993. However, there is no date on it. At least from what I managed to [overlapping speakers].

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LATTANZI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] And the dates next to the names of the Bosniak members, they go as far as the month of July 1993. That would mean that this document dates from a period after July 1993.

utterances.speaker: MR. MUNDIS
utterances.text: If I could be of some assistance. The Prosecution, after we discovered this document, undertook the same kind of quick analysis that Your Honour's doing. I believe, if memory serves me correctly, the person listed as number 26, who has an entry date of 27 August 1993, that's the latest date. So it's actually -- 27 August 1993 is the -- is the latest date, and that's next to person number 26, and so certainly that would give us some indication, but we don't have any precise information as to the date of the document itself.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LATTANZI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: I know you had wished to put in one document before we adjourn, and I know we've gone far beyond the time. Would you like to put that document? Please do.

utterances.speaker: MS. VIDOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honour, no. I'm going to tender this document tomorrow, but I would like to put two very brief questions to the witness and to finish with this topic. They're very short questions, if you permit.

utterances.speaker: MS. VIDOVIC
utterances.text: Please, Witness, now we were just discussing the identity of these people on the list. Would you agree, in any case, that these are not the true identities of the people, the ones that are recorded on this list? Is that correct?

utterances.speaker: AJMAN AWAD [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, I gave an explanation just now as for these names. Within the group, within the detachment, they could recognise each other by our names, these nicknames. As for the corps personnel service and other people who look on, I don't think this is their identity.

utterances.speaker: MS. VIDOVIC
utterances.text: One more short question. It's true, isn't it, that you detachment members did not know the true identities of all the other members of the detachment? And here I'm thinking of the foreigners, not of the Bosnians.

utterances.speaker: AJMAN AWAD [Resumed]
utterances.text: Only the people who were heading the personnel service, who had the documents. When a foreigner would come, he would place his passport, his possessions, items, some money or something. He would give it over for safekeeping, and when he was leaving, he would be given that back. So the only people who knew this were people from the personnel service. I don't know the real names of those people. Sometimes when I hear a name, I really don't know who that is.

utterances.speaker: MS. VIDOVIC
utterances.text: Thank you very much. And the personnel service that kept the documents that were kept in the possession of the El Mujahedin Detachment, that particular archive was never handed over to the Bosnia and Herzegovina authorities?

utterances.speaker: AJMAN AWAD [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, that is correct. This is how I explained that just now.

utterances.speaker: MS. VIDOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, Your Honours. I would now break off here with my cross-examination for today.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Much to the relief of Mr. Awad. We'll take an adjournment --

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: -- until tomorrow at 9.00 in the morning. 9.00 tomorrow morning.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: to be reconvened on Sunday, the 10th day of February, 2008, at 9.00 a.m.
